title: Mathematical morphology can reveal orthogenetic series and warn of convergence

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Mathematical morphology can reveal orthogenetic series and warn of convergence

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Progressive change of growth ratios along a series of allied forms (orthogenesis) is real in some lineages, and the mathematical study of form can detect such series where they are not obvious, while also showing that strong resemblances of form may arise independently as numerical coincidences.

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: And to my mind, the mathematical (as distinguished from the purely physical) study of morphology bids fair to help us to recognise this phenomenon of orthogenesis in many cases where it is not at once patent to the eye; and also, on the other hand, to warn us, in many other cases, that even strong and apparently complex resemblances in form may be capable of arising independently,

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter XI, “The Logarithmic Spiral”; topic “Spiral form and phylogeny”. Scope: fossil and living lineages, especially molluscan shells

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch11-13: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.58

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Directional parameter change and convergence are measurable with public fossil morphology. The broad claim about what mathematical morphology can reveal is partly methodological, and attributing trends to orthogenesis requires substantial interpretation.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Estimate shell growth parameters along independently inferred lineages and test for sustained directional trends, while measuring homoplasy of similar parameter combinations across distant clades. Compare detection against qualitative morphology alone.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Directional trends may reflect sampling, selection or phylogenetic structure.

Orthogenesis has multiple historical and modern meanings.

Independent phylogenies are incomplete for many fossil series.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Convergence of shell form is testable by placing similar geometries on independent trees, and the occurrence, tree and scan resources exist for a molluscan subset. Orthogenesis, as a real directed tendency rather than a description of a trend, has no outcome that current data would assign to it instead of to selection. The usable result is therefore the convergence half and the detection of trends, not the causal status of orthogenesis.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Along fossil and living shell series, test for monotonic change in growth ratios that is not obvious by eye, and test whether similar forms arise in unrelated clades. Independent origins support the convergence warning; a directional ratio trend is compatible with orthogenesis and with selection, so it does not establish orthogenesis.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
The claim that a method can help recognise such series is only partly a claim about nature.

A morphological trend does not separate an internal orthogenetic drive from selection or sampling.
